transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-29
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 52 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Elmrow Head of Platform), Jonas Pettersson (Elmrow Network), Leah Ortiz (Elmrow Security), Marcus King (Product)

Summary:
- Discovery focused on private/VPC onramp for Redwood Private; primary concerns: egress routing, transit gateway peering, cross-region access, and KMS integration.
- Elmrow leaning toward Private deployment behind their VPC, need to validate latency and egress costs.
- Next: network workshop + pilot handshake and share network checklist/terraform examples.

Topics covered: private endpoints, VPC peering vs TGW/transit, private egress strategy (NAT/EDNS), region gating, SOC2/KMS integration, pilot scope and success criteria.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this. Diego, do you want to intro quickly?
[00:10] Diego Alvarez: Yeah hi all, Diego here. I'm the solution engineer, I'll be the tech lead on the network/workshop stuff. Quick note, we'll be scoping network, security and a pilot for latency checks and egress.
[00:22] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. High level — Elmrow is doing more AI inferences on customer data, but we need everything behind our VPC, no public ingress. We're evaluating Redwood Private or a Dedicated instance that sits on our private network. Primary blockers for legal: data residency and audit logs.
[00:38] Maya Chen: Understood. When you say "behind VPC" do you mean a private endpoint that lives in your VPC with direct peering to Redwood, or would you prefer an on-prem gateway?
[00:49] Jonas Pettersson: Prefer VPC peering/Transit Gateway basically. We're on AWS, using TGW for multi-account. We don't want an extra public egress hop. Also concerned about IP ranges and NAT throughput.
[01:05] Leah Ortiz: From security — SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS bring-your-own-key is a hard requirement for production. We also need to know how logs are stored and for how long.
[01:17] Diego Alvarez: That's all typical. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS; for on-prem we can integrate HSMs via standard API. For logs, we push audit logs to a customer S3 or SIEM -- you'll get TTL options.
[01:29] Marcus King: Quick question: what are the differences we should care about between Dedicated versus Private? Latency, cost, and where the control plane runs?
[01:39] Maya Chen: Good question. Short: Dedicated is reserved capacity in our data plane but still talks to Redwood control plane over mutual TLS; it's good for predictable throughput. Private gives you a private control plane option and can be deployed into your VPC or on-prem, so more isolation but slightly longer setup. Diego, add the nuance?
[01:52] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, Dedicated is like reserved GPUs in our infra with isolation, Private actually lets you host the control plane in your account or a customer-managed control plane. That means fewer egress hops and more region control. Setup time for Private is longer, because we do network handshakes and you'll need our installer or terraform module.
[02:06] Jonas Pettersson: And what about inter-region? We run prod in us-east-1 and DR in eu-west-1. We need to keep EU data resident for some customers. Can Redwood service be restricted by region?
[02:18] Diego Alvarez: You can pin model deployments to specific regions. For Private deployments we can deploy nodes only in region X. There's also routing policies to keep traffic local. Small caveat — some open model artifacts may have to be pulled from a central bucket during setup, but we can pre-stage them to eu-west-1 if needed.
[02:34] Priya Nair: That pre-staging detail is important. We can't have cross-border blobs during initial provisioning unless they go to an encrypted pre-stage in the EU.
[02:44] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include a pre-staging flow for eu-west and confirm encryption-at-rest in transit.
[02:50] Marcus King: On egress: what are our options to avoid NAT gateway costs? We already pay a ton for egress out of our VPC.
[03:00] Diego Alvarez: Two main patterns we've seen: 1) Private Endpoint into Redwood inside your VPC and then Redwood routes egress back to your VPC for outbound internet (via your NAT) — you control egress. 2) Use Redwood-managed egress where we handle translucent outbound requests — cheaper operationally but you lose full egress control and might pay Redwood egress charges.
[03:20] Jonas Pettersson: We prefer pattern 1: keep egress in our account. Also need to ensure the KV cache traffic stays inside the VPC — don't want cache hops hitting public nets.
[03:30] Diego Alvarez: KV cache is local to the serving nodes; if nodes are in your VPC, the cache traffic never leaves. Small transcription note: we sometimes say KV "cash" in demos, ha.
[03:37] [laughter]
[03:40] Leah Ortiz: About encryption and KMS — we need BYOK and HSM tie-ins. Is that possible with the Private control plane?
[03:46] Diego Alvarez: Yes. Private supports customer-managed KMS and we can configure the key-encryption so tokens never hit Redwood-managed KMS. HSM integrations are supported through standard KMIP endpoints or cloud KMS with external key control. We'll include a reference doc.
[04:00] Priya Nair: For compliance we also need SIEM integration. Do you push audit logs out-of-band?
[04:05] Maya Chen: We can push audit streams to your S3, or to a streaming endpoint (Kafka/CloudWatch) — Diego will share recommended retention and schema.
[04:12] [00:04:12] Jonas Pettersson: Network specifics — what about peering / TGW? We run TGW and prefer attachments rather than classic VPC peering because we have dozens of accounts.
[04:22] Diego Alvarez: We support TGW attachments. Typical pattern: create a Redwood transit attachment that you accept; routing is via propagated routes in TGW. We'll share terraform snippets. Watchouts: avoid overlapping CIDRs, and ensure MTU is 9001 if you have jumbo frames.
[04:38] Jonas Pettersson: Overlapping CIDRs, yup that's on us — we'll extract our netmap. Also wondering about IP whitelisting: do you ship a list of IP ranges for your nodes so we can update security groups?
[04:48] Maya Chen: Yes, for each Private deployment we'll provide the allocated IP block ranges and ASN info. If you prefer dynamic reference using prefix lists that's doable.
[04:56] Marcus King: Is there any vendor lock we should worry about? If we want to move from Private back to Hosted, is there a data exfil procedure?
[05:05] Diego Alvarez: We'll export models, KV caches dump, and logs. For stateful data we can provide snapshot export. There's an operational playbook for migration. We'll attach that.
[05:15] Leah Ortiz: Latency numbers — demo numbers are great but we need real numbers on our network. Can we run a test harness?
[05:22] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. We'll run an e2e test from your VPC into a pre-provisioned Redwood node in the same region. Test will measure p95 and p99 on cold and warm cache. We typically see p95 token latency under X ms in same AZ — will validate against your topology.
[05:36] Priya Nair: "X ms" is vague, can you give a ballpark for our expected workload? We're doing short responses (<= 256 tokens) at burst QPS up to 120.
[05:45] Diego Alvarez: Ballpark for that profile on gpus we usually recommend quantized Llama-like models with optimized kernels — sub 150ms p95 for short prompts in same AZ. But it depends on batch window and KV sizes. We'll run the pilot.
[05:58] [00:05:58] Jonas Pettersson: Regarding DNS — do you use private hosted zones or something else for the private endpoint?
[06:04] Maya Chen: For Private we create a private endpoint and recommend you add either a private hosted zone that points to the endpoint IPs, or use custom DNS forwarding to our endpoint. Diego to send example Route53 config.
[06:15] Leah Ortiz: On auditing: retention? We need 13 months of logs stored in tamper-evident mode. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[06:23] Diego Alvarez: We can push logs to your S3 with object lock for retention, yes. We'll include the enforcement steps.
[06:29] Marcus King: Pricing sensitivity — what's the cost delta between Dedicated reserved capacity and a Private on-prem-style deployment?
[06:36] Maya Chen: Private has higher setup and infra costs but gives you control; Dedicated is predictable hourly costs with commitment discounts. I'll include a simple TCO doc comparing them.
[06:45] Priya Nair: Important: data residency gating — we must ensure that the inference pipeline for EU customers never leaves eu-west-1.
[06:53] Diego Alvarez: We can do region pinning and restrict rollouts to eu-west-1. If a failover to us-east is needed we can keep cold replicas in the other region but only spin them up under your approval.
[07:05] Jonas Pettersson: Egress again — can Redwood sign BAA or an addendum that clarifies who bears cross-region egress charges?
[07:12] Maya Chen: That's in the enterprise terms. We can add an egress allocation clause to the contract. We'll loop in Legal after the network workshop.
[07:20] [00:07:20] Priya Nair: For pilot success criteria, let's propose: 1) p95 token latency < 200ms for 256-token responses in us-east (local), 2) no traffic leaves customer VPC during the test, 3) KV cache hit-rate > 70% during warm state.
[07:37] Diego Alvarez: Good measurable criteria. We'll map those to test harness metrics and share the script.
[07:44] Marcus King: How long does setup usually take for Private? Two weeks? Longer?
[07:49] Diego Alvarez: Typically 3-6 weeks depending on network approvals and pre-staging artifacts. If you can provision terraform and accept attachments quickly we can accelerate.
[07:59] Leah Ortiz: One more on keys: we keep strict control of KMS key material. We need an architecture note on rotation and access policies.
[08:07] Diego Alvarez: We'll include recommended IAM policies and sample key rotation schedule.
[08:12] [00:08:12] Maya Chen: Ok let's step through a tentative runbook for the pilot: Phase 1: network intake (Jonas shares TGW diagram, CIDRs) Phase 2: pre-stage model artifacts to region Phase 3: deploy test nodes and run harness Phase 4: performance review and go/no-go.
[08:30] Priya Nair: Sounds good. On the networking intake — I'll share our transit topology and security groups. We also have a managed firewall that might block some outbound ports, do you have a port list?
[08:41] Diego Alvarez: We'll provide ports; largely HTTPS (443) and 1024-65535 ephemeral for certain kernels, but we can restrict most control-plane comms to 443. We'll include a minimal port list for the private endpoint.
[08:55] Jonas Pettersson: Can we do BGP peering instead of TGW? We run an on-prem colo that peers via Direct Connect.
[09:02] Diego Alvarez: Yes BGP is supported for direct connects. We'll coordinate ASNs and prefix advertisement.
[09:09] [00:09:09] Marcus King: Any known gotchas you see with companies like us that run strict egress NAT gateways and strict CIDR policies?
[09:17] Diego Alvarez: Overlapping CIDRs, MTU mismatches, and overly restrictive security groups. Also rate-limiting on egress NAT — if your NAT can't sustain burst QPS we recommend provisioned throughput or use an egress VPC with scaled NAT.
[09:30] Priya Nair: For SLA — we need 99.9 for e2e latency and uptime for our production commitment. Is that a conversation for later?
[09:38] Maya Chen: That's typically part of enterprise terms and Dedicated/reserved capacity. We'll surface SLA options in the pricing docs.
[09:44] Leah Ortiz: Compliance — any certifications for the infra used in Private? If we host in our VPC, does Redwood require you to be certed?
[09:51] Diego Alvarez: If nodes run in your VPC and you control the network, the responsibility matrix changes — we'll provide a shared responsibility matrix in the runbook. Redwood infra we manage has SOC 2 Type II; we'll provide the cert.
[09:59] Jonas Pettersson: One small thing: do you support IPv6-only peering? We're considering moving some workloads to IPv6.
[10:06] Diego Alvarez: Partial support today; most customers still use IPv4. We'll check on full IPv6 readiness and note in the workshop.
[10:13] [00:10:13] Maya Chen: Alright, let's do a quick recap and owners. Items to send: network checklist + terraform (Diego), pricing/TCO (Maya), runbook + pilot script (Diego), SOC2 + KMS notes (Maya), Elmrow to share TGW diagram and egress constraints (Jonas/Priya).
[10:32] Priya Nair: We'll aim to share the TGW diagram by 2025-10-02.
[10:37] Marcus King: Can you also include a sample whitelist of IP ranges we can import into our prefix-lists?
[10:42] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll provide the block list for the test nodes and explain how it changes in prod.
[10:47] Leah Ortiz: And one procedural ask: include a security contact for Redwood who we can call during the network window.
[10:52] Maya Chen: I'll include an on-call security contact in the workbook.
[10:56] [00:10:56] Diego Alvarez: A couple more small notes — for model pull pre-staging we recommend signed object URLs and server-side encryption; we'll share the pre-stage script. Also if you plan on heavy embedding workloads, we should size nodes differently.
[11:12] Jonas Pettersson: Noted. Embedding load might be a separate pilot.
[11:16] Priya Nair: Thanks everyone. Good session.
[11:19] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the deeper network workshop for the week of Oct 7.
[11:25] [END]
